one_liner: Byte-sliced Camellia kernels computing S-boxes with AES-NI/VAES/GFNI; 3-19x faster than NTT's table-based reference C.
what_it_does: Standalone Camellia-128/192/256 block encryption and decryption kernels plus vectorized key setup, in GCC assembly (x86-64 AVX/AVX2, AArch64 Neon+AES) and portable C intrinsics (x86 SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX-512, AArch64 CE, POWER8+ VSX crypto, RISC-V RVA23 Zvkb+Zvkned). The API is camellia_keysetup_simd128() into a caller-owned struct camellia_simd_ctx, then fixed-width calls that process exactly 16 blocks (SIMD128) or 32 blocks (SIMD256), plus 1-block constant-time variants taking an nblocks count. There are no modes of operation, no tail handling and no runtime CPU dispatch; each build is a separate test binary.
how_it_is_fast: Camellia's S-boxes share AES's GF(2^8) inversion, so with affine pre- and post-filters (vpshufb nibble lookups, or a single GFNI affine instruction) the S-box layer runs on AES SubBytes via AESENCLAST, with 16 or 32 independent blocks byte-sliced across vector registers to fill the pipelines. GFNI replaces the filter-plus-AES sequence with vgf2p8affineinvqb/vgf2p8affineqb, which is why GFNI builds roughly double VAES builds. The technique is from the author's master's thesis 'Block Ciphers: Fast Implementations on x86-64 Architecture' (pp. 42-50).
when_to_use: A protocol or policy requires Camellia and your mode is parallel: CTR, CBC/CFB decryption, XTS or OCB over at least 16 blocks (256 B) per call.
x86-64 with GFNI (Ice Lake/Tiger Lake and later, Zen 4/Zen 5): SIMD256 GFNI builds reach about 14-19x the table-based C (about 0.92 cycles/byte on Ryzen 9 7900X per the README).

You need a cache-timing-safe Camellia: the vector paths use no secret-indexed tables, unlike the reference's four 1 KiB SP tables; the 1-block SIMD128 variants exist for CBC encryption and single blocks.
AArch64 with Crypto Extensions or POWER8+ where only table-based Camellia exists: 2.2-3.0x in 16-block mode on Cortex-A53/ThunderX2 and about 2.4x on POWER9 per the README.
when_not_to_use: Serial workloads (CBC encryption, single blocks): the constant-time 1-block variants are 1.2x-2.9x slower than the table-based C on most listed CPUs (only AVX-512+GFNI on Tiger Lake is about 1.2x faster).

You want a library rather than kernels: libgcrypt ships the same author's code (cipher/camellia-simd128.h says it is from this repository) with modes, runtime dispatch and an extra GFNI/AVX-512 64-way path, under LGPL-2.1.

You are free to pick the cipher: the best GFNI Camellia figure is about 0.92 cycles/byte on Zen 4, while catalogue entries on other machines show AEGIS-128L near 0.18 and SUPERCOP AES-256-GCM near 0.70 cycles/byte, with authentication included.
RISC-V: the RVA23+Zvkb+Zvkned path was added 2025-12-25 with no published performance numbers and builds with -mstrict-align.

integration.dependencies: none (libc only); GNU make and GCC cross compilers for the provided test binaries
integration.min_toolchain: GCC with the relevant ISA flags (-maes, -mvaes, -mgfni, AVX-512 for the intrinsics builds); README rows cite gcc-13, gcc-14 and gcc-15; Ubuntu 22.04 cross-compilers listed as prerequisites
integration.platforms: x86-64 and i386 (AES-NI with SSE4.1/AVX, AVX2, optional VAES/GFNI/AVX-512), AArch64 with Neon+AES CE, ppc64le POWER8+ with VSX and crypto, riscv64 RVA23 with Zvkb+Zvkned
integration.thread_safety: not documented; all key material lives in the caller-owned struct camellia_simd_ctx and no global mutable state is declared in camellia_simd.h

gotchas: Benchmark noise sets the ratios: main.c times each variant once for 1 s (CLOCK_MONOTONIC, 8 KiB in-place buffer, no repetitions, CPU pinning only in the ThunderX2 sample), and the same camellia_ref_x86-64.o reference reads 372.0 MiB/s in one README sample and 313.4 MiB/s in the other on the same Ryzen 9 7900X (19% apart), so a ratio swings by that much depending on which run it is divided by (the AES-NI SIMD256 sample is 13.9x against 372 but 16.5x against 313).

README sample outputs are older than the code and the bullets: the current intrinsics code always prints a 1-block line (have_camellia_1blk_simd128() returns 1 since the 2025-12-14 commit), yet the test_simd256_intrinsics_x86_64_gfni_avx512 sample has none; the 16-block asm sample gives 3.6x on the 7900X against a ~4.5x bullet, and the Cortex-A53 sample gives 1.26x against a ~2.2x gcc-15 bullet.
Throughput is raw ECB-style block processing on an L1-resident 8 KiB buffer; counter generation, XOR and chaining costs of a real mode are not included.
Argument order is (ctx, out, in), the reverse of the reference's (src, dst), and the 16/32-block functions take no length, so callers must always supply exactly 16 or 32 blocks.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued aead-and-ciphers siblings (libaegis, HiAE, Rocca, intel-ipsec-mb, Crypto++, Botan, Mbed TLS) is a Camellia kernel; pick this only when Camellia is mandated, and pick libaegis or an AES-GCM library whenever the cipher is your choice.
verified_claims_summary: The author's main.c times NTT's camellia-BSD-1.2.0 table-based C (gcc -O2, no -march) against the SIMD kernels, Camellia-128, 8 KiB in place, 1 s per variant: 32-block AVX2/AVX-512+GFNI builds come out about 14-19x faster on Ryzen 9 7900X, Ryzen 9 9950X3D and Core i3-1115G4, AES-NI-only AVX2 builds about 5.4-5.8x on Core i5-6500, and 16-block builds 2.2-4.5x on x86, ARM and POWER9; the README samples I re-derived give 13.9x and 19.1x on the 7900X, but they were run on older code than the bullets.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-01-01, ARMv8 1-block work merged from a contributor), MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but it is a kernel collection with 0 issues filed and 20 stars; libgcrypt's LGPL copy is the maintained production route.
